name: Screen-Understanding GUI Agents
question: Can an agent use an app the way a person does?
summary: A computer-use agent looks at screenshots, decides where to click or what to type, acts through mouse and keyboard actions, and takes another screenshot to check. It can drive legacy desktop or terminal applications that have no API. Each step can fail, and failures compound over long tasks, so reliable GUI agents verify after actions, zoom into small text, use accessibility information where available, and are replaced by an API wherever one exists.
useCases: Legacy back-office apps with no API
Cross-application tasks a person does by hand
Bridging a system until an API is built

steps.title: Give the model a computer
steps.text: The computer-use toolset exposes screenshot, zoom, click, type, key, scroll and wait actions. Your code executes them in a VM.

steps.title: The model looks and decides
steps.text: It reads the latest screenshot and returns the next action, with coordinates in the screenshot’s pixel space.

steps.title: Your code acts
steps.text: The harness performs the click or keystroke in the VM, scaling coordinates back to the real screen.

steps.title: Look again after every action
steps.text: A fresh screenshot shows whether the click worked. Without it, a wrong state goes unnoticed and errors compound.

steps.title: Cap the steps
steps.text: An 18-step task with checks needs about 24 actions; a budget of 20 would run out. Budget for verification.

steps.title: Finish or hand over
steps.text: When the model stops asking for actions, the task is done; if the budget runs out, a person takes over.

practice.scenario: A fictional cooperative bank’s staff re-keyed NEFT return details from emails into a 20-year-old desktop application with no API, about 1,500 cases a month. A computer-use agent in a virtual machine now opens each case, types the fields and takes a screenshot to check each screen before moving on. Without the checks, 40% of cases finished correctly; with verification, zooming into small fields and a 40-step budget, 91% did, and the rest went to staff. The bank has since asked the vendor for an API.

practice.analogy: A temporary clerk using a system for the first time: looks at the screen, clicks, looks again to check it worked, and asks when unsure. Good clerks check every screen; careless ones stack up errors.

library.name: Claude computer use
library.what: The computer-use toolset returns click, type, scroll, zoom and screenshot actions that your code executes in a VM, looping until the task is done.

practice.note: Coordinates refer to the screenshot you returned; scale them back to the VM’s real resolution. Check the current tool version in the docs.

samples.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
TOOLS = [{"type": "computer_toolset_20260801"}]

def run_task(task: str, vm, max_steps: int = 40):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        response = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=2048,
            tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
        results = []
        for block in response.content:
            if block.type != "tool_use":
                continue
            output = vm.execute(block.name, block.input)       # click, type, zoom...
            shot = vm.screenshot(max_long_edge=1568)           # resize before returning
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                            "content": [output, shot]})
        if not results:
            return messages                                    # task finished
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
    raise TimeoutError("step budget exhausted; hand to a person")

numericDrill.question: A GUI task takes 18 actions, and each succeeds independently with probability 0.97. What share of tasks succeed end to end, in percent?
numericDrill.answer: 0.97¹⁸ ≈ 0.578, or about 57.8%. At 0.995 per step it would be about 91.4%. Long tasks need very high per-step accuracy, which is why verifying after each action pays off.

interview.question: When would you use a GUI agent instead of an API?
interview.answer: Only when there is no API or accessible interface: legacy desktop apps, terminals, or portals you cannot integrate with. GUI agents are slower, costlier and less reliable than API calls, so they bridge a gap until an API exists, and they run in a sandboxed VM with verification and a human fallback.

interview.question: Why do GUI agents fail on long tasks?
interview.answer: Errors compound: a small chance of a wrong click or misread field at each step multiplies over dozens of steps. Downscaled screenshots hide small text, and without checking the screen after each action the agent carries on from a wrong state. Verification, zoom, step budgets and shorter tasks all help.
